content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenght:

1. The proposed method is easy/

Weakness:

1. The baselines are weak. I think the authors should compare their method with more self-play methods, such as Neural Population Learning[1] and Prioritized Fictitious Self-play[2].
2. The benchmarks are somewhat easy. I think the author should evaluate their method on more challenging benchmarks, such as Google Research Football [3],  Honor of Kings[4], and DouDizhu[5].

- [1] Liu S, Marris L, Hennes D, et al. NeuPL: Neural Population Learning[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.07415, 2022.
- [2] Vinyals O, Babuschkin I, Czarnecki W M, et al. Grandmaster level in StarCraft II using multi-agent reinforcement learning[J]. Nature, 2019, 575(7782): 350-354.
- [3] Kurach K, Raichuk A, Stańczyk P, et al. Google research football: A novel reinforcement learning environment[C]//Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. 2020, 34(04): 4501-4510.
- [4] Wei H, Chen J, Ji X, et al. Honor of kings arena: an environment for generalization in competitive reinforcement learning[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.08483, 2022.
- [5] Guan Y, Liu M, Hong W, et al. PerfectDou: Dominating DouDizhu with Perfect Information Distillation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.16406, 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a variant of Fictitious Self-Play (FSP) that not only uses a best response computed against the meta strategy of the opponent, but also a best response computed against an adaptive deep RL agent, which can adapt to the best response. The paper first shows that the resulting algorithm falls within the class of Generalized Weakened Fictitious Play algorithms, which are guaranteed to converge to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games. The paper concludes by providing an empirical evaluation of the proposed algorithm on synthetic matrix games, a Leduc poker instance, and a couple of continuous games taken from OpenAI gym.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS

1) The paper is well written.

WEAKNESSES

1) The presentation of the algorithms is hard to follow. I thin that more details are needed.

2) The technical contributions of the paper are very weak. The only proof in the paper shows that the proposed algorithm fails with the class of Generalized Weakened Fictitious Play algorithms, and it is rather trivial.

3) The experimental evaluation is lacking. The results on synthetic games and Leduc are not very appealing, since there it seems that CFR is working way better than the proposed algorithm. The results on continuous games are not very informative, since the authors only use two testbeds. I think that experiments on other settings are needed given that the paper is mainly experimental oriented.

MINOR ISSUES

1) I have some concerns on how you added partial observability to the continuous games in OpenAI gym. Are you sure that your choice makes the problems considerably harder than their perfect observability counterparts?
2) I thin too much space is devoted to describing PPO and SAC algorithms.
3) What is the symbol at the end of p.3 used as a superscript of \mathbb{R}.
4) Algorithm 1, Line 4: Is there a missing utility term?
5) It is not clear to me whether you compared the algorithm based on the number of iterations or the number of best responses computed. At the end of p.5 you wrote you are using the latter, while in the plots you wrote "iterations" as x-axis labels. I think it would be better to use the number of best response computations, since it is more related to computing times.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
CLARITY: The paper is well written, but the inner working of the algorithms is difficult to understand.

QUALITY: The technical contributions are correct but rather trivial, while the experimental evaluation is lacking is many aspects.

NOVELTY: The technical contributions are rather straightforward to derive.

REPRODUCIBILITY: Technical results and experiments are reproducible.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors try to solve the policy overfitting problem when applying DRL algorithms to vanilla FSP. This paper then proposes a method called Adaptive Fictitious Self-Play (AFSP) to train against an adaptive DRL agent which can adapt to the best response. The experiments show that AFSP has lower exploitability than FSP.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The proposed methods have a lower exploitability than the original method under the same iteration.

Weaknesses: Although AFSP performs better than FSP, it is unclear for the training time since there is an additional inner loop in each iteration in both AFP and AFSP algorithms. The time complexity of adaptive algorithms (O(NxM)) is much higher than the original FP algorithm method (O(N)). In Algorithm 3, the inner loop runs several ReinforcementLearning (lines 12 and 13). This seems impracticable to generalize the algorithm to other applications. I didn’t see the number of inner loop episodes in the experiment section. The author should give a clear analysis of the time complexity and description of the experiment settings, like running some experiments for comparing using different numbers of M or comparing these algorithms by training time instead of iterations. Besides, in the experiments of “You Shall Not Pass”, it looks like AFSP only slightly improve over FSP after 60 iterations. I am not sure whether it is worth using AFSP if it may require more time to train. In addition, in the Soccer experiment, the training ends at 14 iterations. Is there any reason for not training more iterations in Soccer?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper provides a detailed related work and background. The experiment section is a bit unclear. For example, Figure 3 and Figure 4 should be reversed based on the order of the subsection. In Figure 2 caption, “We plot exploitability agains the number…” should be “We plot exploitability against the number”. Some information is missing, like the number of inner loop episodes and the training time for each algorithm. In addition, the authors provide the source code for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes AFSP to solve the policy overfitting problem when applying DRL algorithms to vanilla FSP. Experiment results show that AFSP performs better than FSP. However, the time complexity of AFSP is much higher than FSP and the experiment results are not quite convincing as mentioned in “Strength And Weaknesses”.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce a variant of Fictitious Self-play in which an additional opponent is trained against within the inner loop of the rollout. Traditionally FSP learn a best-response to the current population of opponents -  this can introduce simple overfitting to the current population (especially during the beginning of training). The authors argue this by training not only against some linear combination of the population (as in vanilla FSP) but also against a vanilla opponent trained specifically to exploit the current agent during the training step. The trajectory collected from this interaction can be considered a regularisation to stop the main agent from overfitting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
* Intuitive addition 
* Seems to work 

### Weaknesses
* The main gain from this method seems to be that you actually train on more experience per training iteration. To understand this better, it’d be good if you could include plots showing progress per experience trained on / timesteps of gameplay stepped through. Or simply some ablations.

* Alternatively a graph to plot to disentangle performance against a larger population vs the regularizer policy would be useful to show AFSP is improving the agent more.

content.title: AdaptFSP: Adaptive Fictitious Self Play
content.TL;DR: Use deep rl to modify FSP for better performance in continuous control games
content.abstract: Fictitious Self-Play (FSP) is an iterative algorithm capable of learning approximate Nash equilibria in many types of two-player zero-sum games. In FSP, at each iteration, a best response is learned to the opponent's meta strategy. However, FSP can be slow to converge in continuous control games in which two embodied agents compete against one another. We propose  Adaptive FSP (AdaptFSP), a deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm inspired by FSP. The main idea is that instead of training a best response only against the meta strategy, we additionally train against an adaptive deep RL agent that can adapt to the best response. In four test domains, two tabular cases--random normal-form matrix games, Leduc poker--and two continuous control tasks--Thou Shall Not Pass and a soccer environment--we show that AdaptFSP achieves lower exploitability more quickly than vanilla FSP.
